hints: Start by thinking about the end result of each division - does one division keep the cell diploid and the other make haploid cells, and when do homologues actually meet?
Think about what happens to chromatids in both divisions, and whether bacteria with a single circular chromosome without histones can do either type of nuclear division.
walkthrough:
Sort Out Maintaining vs Halving**
Mitosis makes two genetically identical diploid cells, so chromosome number is maintained. Meiosis includes two divisions with only one round of DNA replication, so it halves the number from diploid to haploid. That gives X for meiosis and tick for mitosis.

Pairing, Splitting and Prokaryotes**
Only in prophase I of meiosis do homologous chromosomes pair up to form bivalents for crossing over, so meiosis tick, mitosis cross. Sister chromatids are pulled apart in both - in anaphase of mitosis and in anaphase II of meiosis - so tick for both. Prokaryotes do not do mitosis or meiosis, they divide by binary fission and have no true nucleus or homologous pairs, so cross for both.

Final answer: chromosome number is maintained - meiosis X, mitosis tick; homologous chromosomes pair up - meiosis tick, mitosis X; sister chromatids separate - meiosis tick, mitosis tick; occurs in prokaryotes - meiosis X, mitosis X. All 4 rows correct = 2 marks.

hints: Focus first on what meiosis always does in both humans and plants - think number of products, ploidy and variation.
Now ask what the meiotic product actually is - is a human sperm already the finished gamete, while a pollen grain still has more development to do?
Compare the nuclei inside the finished structures and the order of cell divisions that make them.
Use precise names for the diploid parent cells that enter meiosis in testis versus anther to make your comparison explicit.
walkthrough:
What Meiosis Always Does**
In both cases a diploid parent cell goes through meiosis I and II to give four haploid cells with half the chromosome number. Because of crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment in metaphase I, those four products are genetically different. That is the shared role.

Sperm Is Finished, Pollen Is Not**
In a human male, the four haploid spermatids differentiate directly into sperm, which are the actual male gametes for fertilisation. In a flowering plant, the four haploid microspores from the pollen mother cell divide further and develop into pollen grains, which are multicellular gametophytes. The pollen grain is not itself the gamete, it will later produce the two male gamete nuclei.

Count Nuclei and Order Divisions**
A mature sperm carries a single haploid nucleus plus mitochondria and flagellum for motility. A mature pollen grain typically contains two haploid nuclei, the tube nucleus and the generative nucleus. Linked to this, humans do mitosis first to make many diploid spermatogonia, then a primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis. Plants do it the other way round: the diploid pollen mother cell undergoes meiosis first, then each haploid product undergoes mitosis to build the pollen grain.

Write Paired Comparisons**
For full credit every difference must be comparative, for example sperm has one nucleus whereas pollen has two. Aim for two similarities and two differences to secure four marks.

Final answer: Similarities: both produce 4 haploid cells by meiosis; both halve chromosome number to n / one set; both produce genetically different cells due to crossing over and independent assortment. Differences: human sperm is the male gamete, pollen grain is not a gamete but a male gametophyte that will produce gametes; sperm has one haploid nucleus, pollen grain contains two haploid nuclei (tube and generative); in humans mitotic proliferation then meiosis (spermatogonia by mitosis then primary spermatocyte by meiosis), in plants meiosis then mitosis (pollen mother cell by meiosis then microspore by mitosis).

hints: First check the R locus in each genotype - what happens to all petal and eye colour if R is absent?
If R is present, look next for D and P - remember D masks P when both are present.
Apply that logic to the case with only P present and no D to predict the pale pink case.
Apply the same logic to the case with neither D nor P to see what white with a red eye means.
walkthrough:
Use R As The Master Switch**
R gives red eye pigment and allows D and P to be expressed. If the genotype is rr, no pigments are made at all, so petals are white and there is no red eye, whatever D and P are. That immediately solves rr Dd Pp as white petals, white centre.

Rank D Over P**
When R is present: D plus R gives dark pink petals with red eye. P plus R gives pale pink petals with red eye. When D, P and R are all present, the flower is dark pink with red eye, so D is dominant in effect over P.

Read Each Genotype**
RR dd PP has R and only P, so pale pink petals, red eye. Rr Dd Pp has R, D and P, so dark pink petals, red eye because D masks P. RR dd pp has R but neither D nor P, so no petal pigment but R still gives red eye, so white petals, red eye.
Final answer: RR dd PP - pale pink petals, red eye; Rr Dd Pp - dark pink petals, red eye; rr Dd Pp - white petals, no red eye / white centre; RR dd pp - white petals, red eye.

hints: Start at the DNA level - what kinds of small changes to bases can alter the code read by transcription and translation?
Think how that altered code changes the chain of amino acids and the final 3D shape of the protein.
Consider what happens if the new code introduces an early stop signal during translation.
Link the faulty protein shape to its job in making pigment - why would the whole pathway fail?
walkthrough:
From DNA Change To New Code**
The R to r change is a gene mutation such as substitution, insertion or deletion of bases. Insertion or deletion can cause a frameshift, so every codon downstream is misread.

From New Code To New Protein Shape**
A changed codon sequence puts different amino acids into the primary structure. Different amino acids mean different hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds, so the tertiary 3D shape is altered. If a premature STOP codon is created, translation stops early and the polypeptide is shortened.

From Faulty Enzyme To No Pigment**
The R protein is an enzyme in the pigment biosynthetic pathway. With the wrong shape its active site no longer fits its substrate, so it cannot catalyse its step. The pathway is blocked and no red pigment is synthesised, giving the recessive white phenotype.

Final answer: Mutation is base substitution / insertion / deletion causing frameshift; amino acid sequence / primary structure is changed; tertiary / 3D structure is changed; premature STOP codon gives shortened polypeptide; non-functional enzyme cannot bind substrate so biosynthetic pathway for red pigment does not function.

hints: If the DNA does not code for amino acids, think about what else DNA does to control when and how much a gene is switched on.
walkthrough:
Control Not Code**
Much DNA does not code for polypeptide but controls transcription. A mutation there can alter a promoter, enhancer or other binding site for RNA polymerase or transcription factors, so the pigment gene is not switched on correctly and flower colour changes without changing protein sequence itself.
Final answer: Region is a regulatory sequence / promoter / enhancer / transcription factor binding site that controls expression of the pigment gene.
